**The Fence and the Jacket**

Lena had always been quick on her feet. Whether it was racing her friends to the old oak tree or leaping over puddles after the rain, she prided herself on her agility. But today, her confidence had betrayed her.

She had been cutting through the empty lot behind her neighborhood, a shortcut she took every day after school. The fence between the lot and the next street was low—just a rusted wire barrier—but today, as she jumped, something snagged. A sharp, tearing sound made her stomach drop.

Her dress.

The fabric had caught on a jagged piece of metal, and as she landed on the other side, the sound of ripping echoed in her ears. She turned, heart pounding, and saw the tattered remains of her dress still clinging to the fence. The rest of it—what was left—barely covered her at all.

Heat rushed to her face. She was exposed. Completely exposed.

Lena’s hands flew to her body, trying to cover herself as best as she could. Her backpack was useless—it had fallen on the other side of the fence. She couldn’t go back. She couldn’t stay here. Panic clawed at her throat.

“Oh no, oh no, oh no,” she whispered, pressing herself against the fence, as if it could shield her from the world.

Then she heard footsteps.

Her breath hitched. Someone was coming. She squeezed her eyes shut, wishing she could disappear.

“Hey there,” a gruff but gentle voice said.

Lena didn’t dare look up. She could feel the man’s presence—older, maybe her grandfather’s age. She wanted to sink into the ground.

“You alright?” he asked.

She shook her head, her face burning. She couldn’t speak. What could she possibly say?

A rustling sound. Then, something soft brushed against her shoulder.

“Here,” the man said. “Put this on.”

Lena opened her eyes just enough to see a worn but clean jacket draped over her arms. She fumbled with it, her fingers trembling as she pulled it on. It was too big, swallowing her small frame, but it covered her. The warmth of it—both physical and otherwise—made her throat tighten.

“Thank you,” she whispered, her voice barely audible.

The man nodded, his expression kind. “You need help getting home?”

Lena shook her head again, too embarrassed to explain. She just wanted to vanish.

“Alright,” he said. “You take care now.”

She watched as he walked away, leaving her standing there in his jacket, her cheeks still flushed with shame. But beneath the humiliation, there was something else—a flicker of gratitude.

And for the first time since the fence had torn her dress, she didn’t feel quite so alone.
